title: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates
claim: Under the proposed initialization, feature norms stay invariant to initialization scale, while standard scalings grow and depend on it.
layout: Left architecture diagram with init table; right 2x3 plot grid, shared legend
description: The left half shows a LoRA branch. A large blue box labeled Frozen Pretrained Weight W sits beside two orange trapezoids. The lower one is A and the upper one is B. Each is annotated with a Gaussian initialization that includes the scale beta. Circles for Z_A and Z_B sit between and above them. An input box feeds both paths, and a plus node sums the outputs. Three rounded boxes below list variance settings for Init[A], Init[AB] and Init[A^2]. The n^-2 in the last box is red. The right half is a 2x3 grid of line plots. The columns are the three initializations. The top row plots the Z_A norm and the bottom row plots the Z_B norm over 100 training steps. Dark purple, magenta and orange curves show beta=1, 5 and 25. The curves for Init[A^2] overlap almost exactly, while the other columns spread out or grow. A legend sits at the bottom.
caption: Overview of LoRA initialization and feature-norm stability. Left: LoRA branch notation and the initialization scalings compared in this work, including standard Init[A], Init[AB], and the proposed Init[A2]. Right: feature-norm trajectories at width n = 4096 for different initialization scales β. Init[A2] keeps the LoRA features nearly invariant to β, while the alternative scalings exhibit stronger initialization-dependent growth.
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $Î·_B / Î·_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $Î·_B$, the initialization scale $Î²$, and the adapter rank $r$. In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose \initAA, a simple initialization that scales the variance of $A$ as $Ï_A^2 \propto n^{-2}$ while keeping $B_0=0$. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of $1/n$, stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, \initAA substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, \initAA reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard \initA, and makes the width-based guideline $Î·_B \approx n Î·_A$ a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.
